item.title: How to Run Your Way Through Washington, D.C.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: A 21-mile long run through D.C., from the Capitol and Hains Point to Rock Creek Park and Theodore Roosevelt Island.
item.content:encoded:
Hey runners, if you live in Washington, D.C., or plan to visit, save this article and come back to it before your next long run. Over the past six months, I ran almost 1,000 miles in D.C. while training for the Marine Corps Marathon. Along the way, I had to get creative with my long runs because, as beautiful as the National Mall is, running in a rectangle for hours on end is not fun. So come with me as I take you on the best long run you’ll experience in D.C.

I used Trail Router to build the map below. The entire route is 21 miles, which you could use for your longest run if you’re marathon training, but feel free to adjust any part of it to your needs.

The National Mall

Start outside the Federal Triangle Metro stop and run up Madison Drive toward the Capitol. On the left side of the Capitol, you’ll climb a little hill, but once you’re in front of the building, the view is absolutely worth it.

After you’ve gotten your obligatory Capitol picture, run along 1st Street, where you’ll pass the Supreme Court and the Library of Congress, before looping back along Jefferson Drive toward the Washington Monument.

Once you reach the Washington Monument, which should be around mile 3, take a picture and then head left toward Hains Point.

Hains Point

This might just be the most blissful part of your whole run. Watch the golfers on your right and the water on your left as you jog past all the other serious runners in the city. The loop itself is roughly 3 miles, and I’ll often do multiple laps if I want to stay relatively close to my apartment.

The Tidal Basin and the Lincoln Memorial

When you reach the end of the loop, keep going straight under the bridge, and you’ll come out facing the Tidal Basin. The Tidal Basin is the body of water that’s home to the Jefferson Memorial, the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial and the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial. You’ll also spot the Washington Monument again across the water.

Now head up toward the Lincoln Memorial to finish your time on the National Mall. By now, you should be somewhere between 7 and 9 miles in.

Georgetown and Rock Creek Park

There are several ways to continue your run from here, and each one is scenic and a great way to add mileage. I have us running north through Georgetown toward Rock Creek Park (dots 8, 9 and 10 on the map). I had actually never run in Rock Creek Park until the Marine Corps Marathon, but it was absolutely beautiful, and I’ll be adding it to my future long runs, which is why it’s included here. The entire trail is lined with trees, and you feel like you’re running through a forest. Once you reach a point where you’d like to turn around, head south back toward the Mall. You’ll run through several fun areas on the way.

Kalorama, Dupont Circle and Foggy Bottom

You’ll first run through Kalorama, arguably the nicest neighborhood in D.C. and home to the Obamas, Jeff Bezos and many other political and business figures. Then you’ll run down through Dupont Circle. If you’re doing your long run on a Sunday, this is a great place to stop at the farmers market and grab a bagel or coffee before continuing. Next, you’ll head down through Foggy Bottom. By now, you’ll likely be somewhere between 12 and 15 miles into your run.

The Mount Vernon Trail and Theodore Roosevelt Island

You can stop here, since you’ll be close to the Mall again, or you can add one more stop: the Mount Vernon Trail. To get to the trail, cross the Arlington Memorial Bridge, turn left and take the little loop. If you go north, it’ll take you toward the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial. If you go south instead, you’ll be running toward Hains Point again.

Let’s say you go north. Continue along the trail past the Theodore Roosevelt Bridge, and you’ll see a footbridge on your right that takes you to Theodore Roosevelt Island. The island feels like something out of a fairy tale. Take a minute to explore, and when you’re ready to leave, head north until you reach the Key Bridge, which will take you back into D.C.

The finish

You’ll finally end your run along the Georgetown waterfront, which you can follow east until you get back to your starting point.

Congrats! You just explored most of D.C. and completed your longest run of marathon training!

Let me know what other stops you would add to this route, and I’ll try them out on my next long run.

This story first appeared on vitalityritual.org.
